title: Your Encoder Is a Compromise: The Amortisation Gap

body:
When a textbook introduces the variational autoencoder, the encoder $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ is presented as a neural-network stand-in for the posterior $p(z \mid x)$, trained to minimise $\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| p)$ in expectation over the data. The derivation is clean and the architecture works. What the derivation does not say is that $q_\phi$ has two separate reasons to fall short of the true posterior, and that one of them is specific to the decision to share parameters across all inputs. That second shortfall is the amortisation gap. Cremer, Li, and Duvenaud named it and measured it in 2018, and the number has quietly shaped how approximate Bayesian inference is engineered since.

## Why the split exists at all

Fix a model $p_\theta(x, z) = p(z) \, p_\theta(x \mid z)$ and a datum $x$. The evidence lower bound against any distribution $q(z)$ is

$$\mathcal{L}[q; x] = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\!\left[\log p_\theta(x, z) - \log q(z)\right] = \log p_\theta(x) - \mathrm{KL}\!\left(q(z) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\right).$$

Call the slack $\mathrm{KL}(q \| p(\cdot \mid x))$ the *inference gap* at $x$. It is the amount of log-evidence the bound leaves on the table because $q$ is not the true posterior. Two choices now get stacked into a single $q$: a *family* $\mathcal{Q}$ of candidate distributions (Gaussians with diagonal covariance, say, or a normalising flow), and an *inference function* $\phi \colon x \mapsto q_\phi(\cdot \mid x) \in \mathcal{Q}$ that, given the input, selects one member of that family. The textbook writes both as $q_\phi$.

Let $q^*(z \mid x) \in \mathcal{Q}$ be the member of the family that minimises the inference gap at $x$: the best this family can do if it were allowed to refit from scratch for this one datum. Then

$$\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\left(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z \mid x)\right)}_{\text{inference gap}} = \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\left(q^*(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z \mid x)\right)}_{\text{approximation gap}} + \underbrace{\bigl(\mathcal{L}[q^*; x] - \mathcal{L}[q_\phi; x]\bigr)}_{\text{amortisation gap}}.$$

The decomposition is exact and not symmetric. The approximation gap is the price of restricting to $\mathcal{Q}$; it goes to zero only when $\mathcal{Q}$ contains the true posterior. The amortisation gap is the price of refusing to re-optimise per datum; it goes to zero only when the shared $\phi$ happens to land on $q^*$ for every $x$ in the data distribution. Both terms are non-negative, and either can dominate.

## What changed when the names appeared

Pre-2018, when a VAE under-performed a non-amortised SVI baseline, the response was to enrich the family — add flow layers, inverse-autoregressive transforms, a mixture. The implicit theory was that the posterior family was too narrow. Cremer et al. (2018) ran the comparison end-to-end and found something sharper. On MNIST the two gaps are roughly equal and both small. On Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 — more diverse datasets — the amortisation gap is substantially larger than the approximation one. Enriching the family by stacking normalising-flow layers reduces the inference gap, as expected, but the reduction is primarily in the *amortisation* term, not the *approximation* term. The extra flow parameters, read this way, are doing less to widen the family than they are to give the encoder more routes to a reasonable family member.

The practical reading is that an under-performing VAE on complex data is not usually improved by a wider family on its own. Either the encoder needs to be bigger (shrinking amortisation directly) or the training objective needs to stop treating one feed-forward pass as the final word on the posterior.

## A concrete anchor

A small numerical illustration makes the geometry visible. Consider a mixture-of-two-Gaussians posterior in one dimension, parameterised by $x$:

$$p(z \mid x) = 0.5 \, \mathcal{N}(z;\, -\mu(x),\, 0.3^2) + 0.5 \, \mathcal{N}(z;\, +\mu(x),\, 0.3^2), \qquad \mu(x) = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\sin(3x).$$

Restrict the variational family to single Gaussians: $\mathcal{Q} = \{\mathcal{N}(\mu_q, \sigma_q^2)\}$. For any fixed $x$, the family cannot represent two modes, so the best Gaussian $q^*(\cdot \mid x)$ already incurs an approximation gap. Now define the amortisation function $\phi \colon x \mapsto (\mu_q, \log \sigma_q)$ as a one-hidden-layer MLP, train it to maximise the ELBO averaged over $x \sim \mathrm{Unif}[-\pi, \pi]$, and separately refit $\mu_q, \sigma_q$ per $x$ by numerical optimisation.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

rng = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)

def log_p(z, x):
    mu = 1.0 + 0.5 * torch.sin(3.0 * x)
    sig = 0.3
    log_mix = -0.5 * ((z + mu) / sig) ** 2
    log_mix2 = -0.5 * ((z - mu) / sig) ** 2
    # log-sum-exp of two equal-weight Gaussians
    m = torch.maximum(log_mix, log_mix2)
    return m + torch.log(0.5 * (torch.exp(log_mix - m) + torch.exp(log_mix2 - m))) \
           - torch.log(torch.tensor(sig)) - 0.5 * torch.log(torch.tensor(2 * torch.pi))

def elbo(mu_q, logsig_q, x, K=256):
    sig_q = torch.exp(logsig_q)
    eps = torch.randn(K, *mu_q.shape, generator=rng)
    z = mu_q + sig_q * eps
    log_qz = -0.5 * ((z - mu_q) / sig_q) ** 2 - logsig_q \
             - 0.5 * torch.log(torch.tensor(2 * torch.pi))
    return (log_p(z, x) - log_qz).mean(0)

# Amortised encoder (shared across x)
enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 64), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(64, 2))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(enc.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for _ in range(4000):
    x = (torch.rand(128, 1, generator=rng) * 2 - 1) * torch.pi
    out = enc(x)
    mu_q, logsig_q = out[:, 0:1], out[:, 1:2]
    loss = -elbo(mu_q, logsig_q, x).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

# Compare on a grid of x
xs = torch.linspace(-torch.pi, torch.pi, 25).unsqueeze(1)
with torch.no_grad():
    out = enc(xs); L_amort = elbo(out[:, 0:1], out[:, 1:2], xs, K=4096)

L_star = torch.zeros_like(L_amort)
for i, x in enumerate(xs):
    mu_q = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)
    logsig_q = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)
    o = torch.optim.Adam([mu_q, logsig_q], lr=5e-2)
    for _ in range(1500):
        o.zero_grad()
        (-elbo(mu_q.view(1, 1), logsig_q.view(1, 1), x.view(1, 1))).backward()
        o.step()
    L_star[i] = elbo(mu_q.view(1, 1), logsig_q.view(1, 1), x.view(1, 1), K=4096).squeeze()

print("mean amortisation gap:", (L_star - L_amort).mean().item())
```

Two things to notice. The per-datum optimum $q^*(\cdot \mid x)$ still cannot cover the bimodal posterior — that residual is the approximation gap, visible in the absolute ELBO deficit at any $x$. But the shared encoder cannot even reach $q^*$ uniformly in $x$: the function from $x$ to the best Gaussian wiggles with $\mu(x)$, and a modest MLP trained on expected ELBO averages across $x$ rather than solving for each one. The difference $\mathcal{L}[q^*] - \mathcal{L}[q_\phi]$ is strictly positive and fluctuates with $x$ in a way the family-restriction alone does not explain.

## When amortisation is the ceiling and when it is not

The clean diagnostic is Cremer et al.'s own: train an inference network, then at convergence take each $x$ in a held-out set, initialise $(\mu_q, \log \sigma_q)$ from $q_\phi(\cdot \mid x)$, and run stochastic variational inference to refine. The improvement in ELBO is a direct estimate of the amortisation gap at that point. On MNIST the improvement is modest; on Fashion-MNIST or CIFAR-10 it tends to be large. Margossian and Blei (UAI 2024) later gave sufficient conditions under which a sufficiently flexible inference network can close the gap entirely in the population limit, and pointed to hidden Markov models as a case where the gap is irreducible for structural reasons: the sufficient statistic that would drive $\phi$ is not a function of $x_t$ alone.

The semi-amortised fixes follow the diagnostic. Kim et al. (ICML 2018) initialise with $q_\phi$ and run a handful of per-datum SVI updates, differentiating through the refinement so the encoder is trained to produce good starting points. Marino, Yue, and Mandt (ICML 2018) make the iteration explicit: the inference network takes gradients of the ELBO as input and learns to perform the refinement itself, generalising the standard encoder as a one-step case. Both approaches tighten the bound and, in text models in particular, mitigate the posterior-collapse pathology that Kim et al. link back to a propagating amortisation error — a bad $q_\phi$ feeds misleading gradients into $\theta$, which encourages $\theta$ to route information around $z$ rather than through it.

## What to do with this in practice

The amortisation gap is worth separating from two neighbours it is often confused with.

It is not the ELBO itself. Report two numbers: the amortised ELBO, and the test-time refined ELBO. The second is the ceiling your family imposes; the first is the ceiling your encoder imposes. Their difference is the amortisation gap, and it is a distinct lever from family capacity.

It is not posterior collapse. Collapse is $q_\phi(z \mid x) \approx p(z)$ for every $x$, which registers as $\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| p) \approx 0$ in the ELBO. A model can suffer collapse even with a flexible family, because the pathology is in the training dynamics; a model can suffer a large amortisation gap without collapsing. The two interact — a chronic amortisation gap feeds back through $\theta$ and can nudge the model toward collapse — but they are not the same object.

It is not purely an encoder-capacity question. Doubling encoder width helps, but with diminishing returns once the function $x \mapsto q^*(\cdot \mid x)$ is genuinely hard to approximate — think images, long documents, structured observations. At that point the right move is to stop asking a feed-forward pass to be the final answer. A few SVI updates per minibatch, warm-started by the encoder and differentiated through, is a cheap intervention.

## Limits and open questions

The decomposition assumes $q^*$ is well-defined, which requires reaching the global optimum within $\mathcal{Q}$ for each $x$ to any desired precision. In practice the "per-datum refinement" step is itself an optimiser with its own tolerance and its own local minima, especially for non-mean-field families. Ganguly et al.'s 2023 review documents how fragile the measured amortisation gap can be to choices of refinement budget. An apparent gap can be inflated by under-refining $q^*$.

Second, the empirical story is dominated by image VAEs and short-text LSTMs. Transformer-based latent-variable models with discrete bottlenecks and hierarchical latents complicate the arithmetic. It is not obvious that the 2018 finding — amortisation dominates approximation on complex data — generalises mechanically to every modern setup, and there has been no systematic re-measurement at scale that I could cite with confidence.

Third, the Margossian-Blei result tells us that the gap closes in principle under conditions on the model class. Whether realistic encoders satisfy those conditions on realistic data is an open empirical question, and the proposed check — a few MFVI steps after AVI convergence, see if ELBO improves — is only diagnostic, not prescriptive.

The compression you got when you decided to share an encoder across data points was not free. Measuring its price requires one extra line of per-datum optimisation at evaluation time, and most of what has been built in approximate inference since 2018 is an answer to the number that line returns.

## Further reading

- Chris Cremer, Xuechen Li, David Duvenaud, "Inference Suboptimality in Variational Autoencoders", arXiv:1801.03558, ICML 2018. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.03558>. The paper that named and measured the gap; the Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR numbers are the empirical hinge for everything downstream.
- Yoon Kim, Sam Wiseman, Andrew C. Miller, David Sontag, Alexander M. Rush, "Semi-Amortized Variational Autoencoders", arXiv:1802.02550, ICML 2018. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.02550>. The cleanest fix: amortised initialisation plus differentiated SVI refinement, with the posterior-collapse argument spelled out for text.
- Joe Marino, Yisong Yue, Stephan Mandt, "Iterative Amortized Inference", arXiv:1807.09356, ICML 2018. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.09356>. Makes the amortised encoder a learned optimiser that consumes gradient information; standard VAEs recover as the one-step case.
- Charles C. Margossian, David M. Blei, "Amortized Variational Inference: When and Why?", arXiv:2307.11018, UAI 2024. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11018>. The more recent theoretical sharpening: sufficient conditions for the gap to close, counterexamples when it cannot, and a cheap diagnostic.
- Ankush Ganguly, Sanjana Jain, Ukrit Watchareeruetai, "Amortized Variational Inference: A Systematic Review", Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 78 (2023). <https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/14258>. A readable survey of the gap, collapse, and the semi-amortised landscape; useful as an index into the literature after 2018.
